intro: The first movement of Haydn’s Symphony No. 94, the “Surprise”, opens with a quiet exchange between winds and strings; at the Vivace assai two violins begin the quick movement before the full orchestra enters. Serge Koussevitzky conducts the Boston Symphony Orchestra in this 1929 recording.

sections.label: Intro · Adagio cantabile, winds and low strings
sections.mNote: Short phrases in G major before the Vivace assai

sections.label: A · Two violins, then the orchestra
sections.mNote: Vivace assai; after the quiet opening, the orchestra plays in G major.

sections.label: Dev · Opening theme in new keys
sections.mNote: The violins play broken chords through minor keys.

sections.label: A′ · B minor, returning to G major
sections.mNote: The repeated B becomes part of the G major tonic chord.

cues.title: Opening phrases, winds and strings
cues.text: A two-bar phrase in the winds is followed by a two-bar phrase in the low strings. The strings move towards D major, and when the exchange is repeated they return to G. Haydn marked the passage Adagio cantabile.
cues.evidence: Adagio cantabile, bars 1–17, described in the movement-by-movement score discussion: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Slow introduction
cues.text: Every London symphony except No. 95 begins with a slow introduction. Orrin Howard described this one as “a brief, patrician prelude” with a passing grey cloud that darkens the horizon. No. 95, the only one in a minor key, has no introduction.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard, LA Phil programme note: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise. Richard Wigmore on No. 95, booklet for Howard Shelley’s recording of the London symphonies (Hyperion, 2009): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/44371-B.pdf

cues.title: Opening of the Vivace assai
cues.text: The Vivace begins in the two violin sections, with a G♯ in the second violins’ first bar pointing towards A minor. Four bars into the new tempo the full orchestra arrives forte on G. The bass holds that G while the notes above it grow quicker.
cues.evidence: Vivace assai, bars 18–30: violin opening, tonic arrival in bar 22 and held G in the bass: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn). The Breitkopf & Härtel full score (ed. Rietz, plate 8876; IMSLP #546546), printed p. 2, read: the second violins’ first bar carries a G♯, and the forte tutti on G arrives four bars in. Richard Wigmore, booklet for Howard Shelley’s recording (Hyperion, 2009), p. 6: the Vivace “initially pretends it is in A minor rather than G major”: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/44371-B.pdf (opened). Orrin Howard, LA Phil programme note: the first theme “begins mischievously outside the home key”: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise (opened).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, London, 1792
cues.text: The symphony was first performed on 23 March 1792, in a concert organised by Johann Peter Salomon during Haydn’s first London visit. Haydn’s pupil Ignaz Pleyel was providing music for a rival concert series in the city.
cues.evidence: Première date: Richard Wigmore, booklet for Howard Shelley’s recording (Hyperion, 2009), p. 6, “Premiered in Salomon’s concert on 23 March 1792”: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/44371-B.pdf (opened). Salomon’s concerts and Pleyel’s rival engagement: Orrin Howard, LA Phil programme note, https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise (opened).

cues.title: Three themes in the exposition
cues.text: Orrin Howard identified three themes in the exposition. He called the first whimsical, noting that it begins “mischievously outside the home key”. He described the second as a restrained, pure waltz tune with a lilt, and the third as a warm melody with distinctive downward leaps.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard, LA Phil programme note: https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise

cues.title: Morning Herald review of the première
cues.text: After the première the Morning Herald’s critic called the subject “remarkably simple, but extended to vast complication”. Richard Wigmore applied this to the movement. The repeated notes and rising chromatic lines of the slow introduction return as material in the quick Vivace.
cues.evidence: Richard Wigmore, booklet for Howard Shelley’s recording of the London symphonies (Hyperion, 2009), quoting the Morning Herald: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/44371-B.pdf

cues.title: Development, Vivace assai
cues.text: The development begins with a variant of the first tune. At bar 123 loud broken chords take over, moving from A major through D minor and B♭ major to G minor.
cues.evidence: Vivace assai, bars 107–140; the broken-chord passage begins at bar 123. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Retransition and recapitulation
cues.text: The development ends with a cadence in B minor. Haydn repeats the note B, then puts G beneath it, so that the same note now belongs to G major. The recapitulation of the first theme begins at bar 154.
cues.evidence: Vivace assai, end of development and recapitulation from bar 154: B minor cadence and repeated B sounding with G. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Haydn’s answer to Griesinger
cues.text: Griesinger asked Haydn, in jest, whether the Andante’s drum stroke was meant to wake dozing Englishmen. Haydn said he had wanted to surprise the public and debut brilliantly, so that his pupil Pleyel should not outdo him. The first Allegro, he added, had already won countless bravos.
cues.evidence: Georg August Griesinger, Biographische Notizen über Joseph Haydn (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1810), the recollections of Haydn’s English stay that follow his own list of works. Haydn’s answer to the question about the drum-stroke Andante: “um mir nicht den Rang von Pleyel, meinem Schüler, ablaufen zu lassen”, with Pleyel’s concerts opening “acht Tage” before his own; and “Das erste Allegro meiner Symphonie wurde schon mit unzähligen Bravos aufgenommen”. Bayerische Staatsbibliothek scan, OCR text read at https://archive.org/stream/10600112bsb/10600112bsb_djvu.txt (translation ours). Pleyel’s competing series: Orrin Howard, LA Phil programme note, https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise (opened).

cues.title: Recapitulation of the first movement
cues.text: The return of the main theme brings what Richard Wigmore called, in effect, “an intensive second development”. The theme reaches a rounded conclusion only towards the end.
cues.evidence: Richard Wigmore, booklet for Howard Shelley’s recording of the London symphonies (Hyperion, 2009), on the recapitulation of the first movement: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/44371-B.pdf

transitions.title: From the Adagio introduction to the Vivace
transitions.from: Intro · Adagio cantabile, winds and low strings
transitions.to: A · Two violins, then the orchestra
transitions.how: The introduction ends on a dominant seventh on D. The first violins lead into the Vivace with falling quavers, and the metre changes from 3/4 to 6/8. Both violin sections begin the Vivace on their own. Four bars later the full orchestra enters forte on G, and the bass holds the G for nine bars.
transitions.evidence: Adagio cantabile and Vivace assai, bars 1–30, especially the dominant seventh, falling violin figure and tonic arrival in bar 22. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: From exposition into development
transitions.from: A · Two violins, then the orchestra
transitions.to: Dev · Opening theme in new keys
transitions.how: In the Vivace assai (bars 99–153), the exposition closes in D major and thins to repeated B notes in the first violins. The development opens with a variant of the first tune. The broken chords that follow start abruptly on A major and move through D minor, B♭ major and G minor before a chromatic descent.
transitions.evidence: Vivace assai, end of exposition and development, bars 99–153. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: Recapitulation of the first theme
transitions.from: Dev · Opening theme in new keys
transitions.to: A′ · B minor, returning to G major
transitions.how: A descending chromatic passage reaches F♯ major and then resolves to B minor. The repeated B notes continue. G is added to them, which makes B the third of the home chord. The first theme returns in G major with its repetitions shortened.
transitions.evidence: Vivace assai, bars 134–154 and the recapitulation: F♯ major, B minor and the concealed return to G. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

source.title: Haydn, Symphony No. 94, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, ed. Rietz, plate 8876, [1855])
source.locator: Adagio cantabile — Vivace assai, printed pp. 1–18: wind-and-string introduction, violin opening and orchestral returns.

timeline.note: Oboes and bassoons play above a held horn note. The low strings answer, and a flute joins the repeated wind phrase.
The two violin sections begin the Vivace quietly on their own.
The full orchestra enters forte on G, with trumpets and timpani.
The first tune returns in G major; the full orchestra follows the violin opening.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 22 and 24 April 1929: the first side on 22 April, the second side on 24 April
fields.note: Young’s discography lists the first side (CVE-48983-2) with the 22 April 1929 session and the second side (CVE-48986-2) with a later recording date of 24 April 1929 for the published retaken side. DAHR’s list for 24 April 1929 includes CVE-48986 and Bolig gives take 2 for the second side. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
fields.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1: CVE-48983, take 2 (22 April 1929); side 2: CVE-48986, take 2 (24 April 1929)
fields.note: Young gives CVE-48983-2 and CVE-48986-2 as the issued takes of the first movement’s two sides. Bolig independently gives CVE-48986 take 2 for part 2. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Processing

fields.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

fields.note: Haydn died in 1809. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he wrote in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three. He was a wheelwright’s son and had spent most of his adult life in the livery of a servant of the Esterházy family.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. As a chorister he sang church music daily but received little instruction in composition. Performances outside the cathedral also gave him chances to get a meal. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
